structure.rationale: The ten user-supplied chapters (kept in the requester's order) move from the frame to the machinery to the system: first the architectural principles every later trade-off is judged against (layering, end-to-end, fate sharing, control/data/management planes, per Saltzer-Reed-Clark and Clark '88); then the data plane inside one box (forwarding), then how many boxes agree on paths (routing), then how endpoints share those paths (transport) and how the network arbitrates contention (queues, AQM, scheduling, QoS). Security follows once the reader knows every mechanism an attacker can abuse. SDN, virtualization/cloud and wireless/edge are three re-arrangements of the same planes under new constraints (central control, multi-tenancy, scarce and moving capacity). Measurement and operations close the loop and host the capstone case studies, which reuse every earlier chapter.
structure.audience: Expert readers who already understand fundamental networking (packets, IP addressing, the layer model, basic TCP); they want architectural trade-offs, protocol internals, quantitative reasoning, security, virtualization and operational practice — delivered in the thing-explainer plain-words voice without losing technical precision.

crossChapterThreads.case-studies: measurement-operations-future's capstones (hyperscale DC, global CDN, enterprise zero-trust, 5G edge) cite back to the chapter that owns each mechanism

claims.text: Layering gives each layer a service interface to the one above and hides how the layer below works, so implementations can change independently; the Internet's stack is often drawn as an hourglass with IP as the narrow waist.

Akhshabi & Dovrolis's EvoArch model reproduces the hourglass shape from almost any starting stack; the surviving waist protocols (IPv4; TCP and UDP) are old and widely depended on, not necessarily the highest-quality ones.

RFC 1958 (Carpenter, 1996) summarizes the community view: the goal is connectivity, the tool is the Internet Protocol, and the intelligence is end to end rather than hidden in the network; it notes the Internet grew by evolution, not from a grand plan.

The end-to-end argument (Saltzer, Reed, Clark 1984): a function that can be completely and correctly implemented only with knowledge at the endpoints cannot be provided correctly by the communication system alone; low-level versions are justified only as performance enhancements.

The paper's careful-file-transfer example: threats include disk faults, buffering/copy bugs in host software, and host crashes, which per-hop network reliability cannot catch; the robust fix is an end-to-end checksum check and retry. Making each step triple-redundant is judged uneconomical.

Clark (1988) lists the DARPA Internet's goals in priority order: survivability despite loss of networks/gateways; multiple types of service; variety of networks; distributed management; cost effectiveness; low-effort host attachment; accountability. The ordering came from the military context, and the later goals were met least well.
Fate-sharing (Clark 1988): keep connection state at the endpoints, so state is lost only if the entity that cares about it is also lost; gateways can then be stateless datagram switches.

Clark (1988) records that TCP and IP were originally one protocol and were split so that services not wanting reliable byte streams (e.g. packet voice, debugging) could run over IP via UDP — the 'multiple types of service' goal.

In October 1986 the Internet suffered the first of a series of congestion collapses: throughput between LBL and UC Berkeley (sites about 400 yards apart) fell from 32 kb/s to 40 b/s. The fix (slow start, congestion avoidance, better RTT estimation) was placed in end hosts' TCP, not in routers.

RFC 3439 (Bush & Meyer, 2002) names complexity the main barrier to scaling and states a Simplicity Principle, an Amplification Principle (large systems show non-linearities small ones don't; small things can cause huge events) and a Coupling Principle; its section 3 is 'Layering Considered Harmful', warning that stacking layers adds optimization and feature-richness costs.

Cross-layer designs can create unplanned feedback loops and interaction effects that threaten stability, and unstructured cross-layer coupling produces 'spaghetti' architectures that are hard to maintain and that block later innovation.

RFC 7426 separates the forwarding (data) plane, which handles packets per their rules, from the control plane, which decides those rules for one or more devices, and from the management plane, which monitors, configures and maintains devices; it also names an operational plane for a device's overall operating state, and contrasts control vs management by timescale.

Middleboxes constrain protocol evolution: Honda et al. measured paths that rewrite initial sequence numbers, strip or pass unknown TCP options and resegment data, so new TCP extensions (e.g. MPTCP) must be designed to survive them — 'ossification'.
Encrypting transport headers (as QUIC does) helps avoid ossification by middleboxes and hides transport behaviour from the path, at the cost of operator visibility.

RFC 9413 (IAB, 2023) argues that tolerating unexpected input under the robustness principle ('be conservative in what you send, liberal in what you accept') causes long-term interoperability harm, and recommends active protocol maintenance instead.

Tussle in Cyberspace: stakeholders (users, ISPs, governments, rights holders) have conflicting interests; the architecture should 'design for variation in outcome' — modularize along tussle boundaries and design for choice — rather than dictate one outcome, because rigid designs get broken.

Per-frame overhead for TCP over Ethernet with a 1500-byte MTU: 8 B preamble/SFD + 14 B header + 4 B FCS + 12 B inter-frame gap = 38 B on the wire; IPv4 20 B + TCP 20 B + timestamps 12 B leave 1448 B of payload, so goodput is 1448/1538 ≈ 94.1% of line rate; a 100-byte application message is ≈ 52.6%.

Retry cost arithmetic: with n hops each losing a packet with probability p, end-to-end-only retry succeeds per attempt with probability (1-p)^n and costs on average ((1-(1-p)^n)/p)/(1-p)^n link transmissions, versus n/(1-p) with per-hop retry. n=10,p=1%: 10.6 vs 10.1; n=10,p=10%: 18.7 vs 11.1; n=5,p=30%: 16.5 vs 7.1. This is why lossy links (e.g. Wi-Fi) add link-layer retransmission as a performance enhancement while TCP keeps the end-to-end check.

Availability arithmetic: five components in series at 99.9% each give ≈ 99.50%; two such paths in parallel give ≈ 99.9975% only if their failures are independent — shared fate (same conduit, same software bug, same config push) erases the gain.
Data-plane time budget at 400 Gb/s: a full 1538-byte on-wire frame lasts ≈30.8 ns and a minimum 84-byte on-wire frame ≈1.7 ns, so per-packet work must be fixed-function or pipelined.
Routers police the traffic punted from the data plane to the control-plane CPU (control-plane protection / policing), because flooding that path starves routing protocols.
QUIC connection IDs let a connection survive address changes and let load balancers route without per-connection memory of the 5-tuple.

pitfalls: Reading the end-to-end argument as 'never put function in the network' — the paper explicitly allows in-network versions as performance enhancements; it says they cannot replace the endpoint check.

Treating the OSI 7-layer model as the Internet's architecture; the Internet's working shape is the hourglass around IP, and real systems routinely violate strict layering (NAT, PMTUD, TCP checksum over an IP pseudo-header).
Assuming redundant paths are independent; shared conduits, software and config pushes create correlated failures.
Equating SDN's control/data separation with 'centralization' — the separation is about interfaces; a separated control plane can still be distributed.
Assuming cross-layer optimization is free: it couples layers, creates feedback loops, and freezes the interface it peeks through.

claims.text: A forwarding element's per-packet pipeline is: parse headers, classify/look up (exact, longest-prefix, ternary matches), modify (rewrite MAC, decrement TTL, push/pop labels), then queue and schedule onto the output port; the control plane only fills the tables.
Minimum-size Ethernet frame is 64 B plus 8 B preamble/SFD and 12 B inter-frame gap = 84 B (672 bits) on the wire; at 100 Gb/s that is ~148.8 M packets/s, ~6.7 ns per packet; at 400 Gb/s ~1.68 ns.

Longest-prefix match: an IP destination may match several prefixes; the most specific (longest) wins. The global IPv4 BGP table passed one million prefixes in 2025 (APNIC counted 1,001,332 on 8 May 2025), and the count varies by vantage point.

DIR-24-8 (Gupta, Lin, McKeown 1998): a 2^24-entry first table indexed by the top 24 address bits, plus a second table for longer prefixes; most lookups take one memory access, the rest two; the first table is ~32 MB. DPDK's LPM library uses a variant.

A TCAM stores value+mask per entry and compares the key against every entry in parallel in one cycle; a priority encoder returns the first match, so storing prefixes ordered by length gives longest-prefix match in one access, but inserts may have to move entries to keep the order.

TCAM costs several times more area per bit than SRAM and burns far more power because every search charges every match line; one model gives ~3 µW per bit, and an 18 Mb TCAM at 100–150 MHz is quoted at 10 W or more versus 1–2 W for SRAM.

Exact-match tables (MAC, five-tuple flow tables) are built from hashing into SRAM; ECMP picks among equal-cost next hops by hashing flow fields (hash-threshold in RFC 2992), keeping a flow on one path to avoid reordering at the cost of uneven load when flows differ in size.

With one FIFO per input, head-of-line blocking limits throughput of an N×N input-queued switch under uniform saturated traffic to 2 − √2 ≈ 58.6% as N grows large (Karol, Hluchyj, Morgan 1987); for small N it is higher (0.75 at N=2, ~0.655 at N=4, ~0.618 at N=8).

Virtual output queues (one queue per output at each input) remove HOL blocking; iSLIP, an iterative round-robin matching scheduler, reaches 100% throughput for uniform traffic and never starves a queue; schedulers were built for 32 ports at ~100 M decisions/s.
Pure output queueing needs the output memory to accept up to N packets per slot (N× speedup), which is why high-port-count switches use input/VOQ or shared-memory designs with modest fabric speedup.

Store-and-forward receives the whole frame and checks the FCS before sending, adding one serialization delay per hop (1500 B at 10 Gb/s = 1.2 µs); cut-through starts sending after the header, so latency is roughly independent of frame length, but corrupt frames propagate and cut-through is impossible when the egress is faster than the ingress or the egress is busy.

The buffer rule of thumb is RTT × C; Appenzeller et al. showed a link carrying n long-lived desynchronized TCP flows needs about RTT × C / √n, e.g. a 2.5 Gb/s link with 10,000 flows could cut buffers ~99%; the 2019 Redux paper notes the result changed practice only partly.

RMT (Bosshart et al. 2013): a programmable parser plus 32 physical match-action stages on a 1 GHz pipeline handling 960 M packets/s for 64×10 Gb ports; tables in each stage are built from SRAM (exact match) and TCAM (ternary) blocks; the authors estimate programmability costs ~15% chip area and ~12% power over a fixed-function chip.

P4_16 programs declare headers, a parser state machine, match-action tables with actions, and control blocks that apply tables; the architecture (e.g. v1model, PSA, TNA) fixes what blocks a target exposes. The current spec is v1.2.5 (2024).

Intel announced in January 2023 it would stop developing new Tofino switch ASICs while continuing to sell and support Tofino and Tofino 2; P4 remains used on SmartNICs/DPUs, FPGAs and software targets.
Fixed-function merchant switch ASICs keep doubling: Broadcom's Tomahawk 6 (shipping from June 2025) is a single-chip 102.4 Tb/s switch with up to 512×200G or 1024×100G ports.

SmartNICs/DPUs put programmable packet engines plus general-purpose cores (e.g. NVIDIA BlueField-3: Arm cores, up to 400 Gb/s) on the NIC, so the host's infrastructure work — virtual switching, encryption, storage — runs off the host CPU; AMD Pensando and Intel IPUs are similar parts.

Line-rate hardware is a fixed budget per packet: each pipeline stage gets a fixed number of clock cycles and a fixed number of memory accesses, so programs that need loops, unbounded state or many dependent lookups do not fit; this is why P4 has no loops in the control flow and parsers are bounded state machines.

On 12 August 2014 ('512K day') the IPv4 table briefly passed 512,000 routes after a burst of ~15,000 deaggregated routes; older routers whose default hardware (TCAM) partition held ~512K IPv4 routes overflowed, causing scattered outages, though the vendor had warned beforehand and the fix was a reconfiguration plus reboot.

Packets a hardware parser cannot handle at line rate (e.g. IPv4 options, unusually deep header stacks) are typically punted to a slower CPU path or dropped, which discourages new header formats in the middle of the network.
Broadcom also ships a co-packaged-optics Tomahawk 6 variant (Davisson), moving optical I/O next to the switch die to cut I/O power.
Derived figure: a 102.4 Tb/s chip at 672 bits per minimum-size packet would face ≈1.52×10^11 packets/s if every port ran smallest packets.

pitfalls: Line rate is usually quoted for large packets; small-packet (64 B) rates are the hard case and many boxes cannot do them on every port at once.
The FIB (in the data plane) is not the RIB (in the control plane); a router can hold more routes in software than its hardware tables fit, and overflow means slow-path or dropped traffic.
58.6% is the large-N, uniform, saturated, fixed-cell limit; real HOL loss depends on traffic.
Cut-through only helps when the output is idle and no faster than the input; under load every switch is store-and-forward.
RTT×C/√n assumes many desynchronized long flows; it does not apply to data-center incast or links with few flows.
ECMP hashing keeps flows in order but a few elephant flows can collide on one link; same hash function on every tier causes polarization.

routing-algorithms-protocols-policy.fetchNote: rfc-editor.org and datatracker were unreachable through the build proxy on 2026-11-14; RFC facts were cross-checked via search snippets of the RFC text, vendor docs and course notes, plus long-stable textbook knowledge.

claims.text: Distance-vector routing (distributed Bellman-Ford): each router tells its neighbors its current best distance to every destination and takes min(link cost + neighbor's distance); it never sees the topology.

After a failure, distance-vector can 'count to infinity': routers keep raising their distances via each other's stale reports. RIP caps the metric at 16 = unreachable, limiting the network to 15 hops; it sends full updates every 30 s.

Split horizon: do not advertise a route back out the interface it was learned on; poisoned reverse: advertise it back with metric 16. These fix two-node loops but not every loop of three or more routers under unlucky timing.

Link-state routing: every router floods a description of its own links (LSAs in OSPF, LSPs in IS-IS) to all routers in the area; each builds the same map and runs Dijkstra's shortest-path-first locally.

OSPF runs over IP (protocol 89), uses a two-level hierarchy of areas around a backbone area 0, and areas summarize to bound flooding and SPF cost. IS-IS runs directly over the link layer, not IP, encodes data in extensible TLVs, and uses level-1/level-2 hierarchy; large ISPs often favor IS-IS.

Francois, Filsfils et al. (2005) measured link-state operations on deployed routers and concluded sub-second IGP convergence is achievable in large ISP networks without compromising stability; RIB/FIB update of many prefixes, not SPF itself, tends to dominate.

Path-vector (BGP): advertisements carry the full list of ASes the route has passed (AS_PATH); a router rejects any route containing its own AS, which prevents loops without a global map, and lets each AS apply its own policy.
BGP runs over TCP port 179; it sends incremental UPDATEs (announcements and withdrawals), not periodic full tables.

BGP route selection: first highest LOCAL_PREF (the local 'degree of preference'), then shortest AS_PATH, lowest ORIGIN (IGP<EGP<incomplete), lowest MED (compared by default only among routes from the same neighboring AS), eBGP over iBGP, lowest IGP cost to the next hop, then lowest BGP identifier. Vendors add steps (e.g., Cisco weight before LOCAL_PREF).
iBGP speakers do not re-advertise routes learned from one iBGP peer to another, so plain iBGP needs a full mesh: n routers need n(n-1)/2 sessions (100 routers → 4,950).

Route reflection (RFC 4456): a route reflector re-advertises iBGP routes to its clients; ORIGINATOR_ID records the router that injected the route, CLUSTER_LIST records the reflection path, and both are used to drop looped advertisements. A reflector passes on only its own best path, which hides alternatives from clients.

RFC 3345: with single-level route reflection or confederations and MEDs from two or more neighbor ASes for one prefix, BGP can oscillate persistently; mitigations include deterministic MED ordering and always-compare-MED. It is a case of locally sensible policies conflicting globally.

Gao-Rexford conditions: prefer customer routes over peer/provider routes; export customer routes to everyone but peer/provider routes only to customers; no cycles of provider-customer links. If every AS follows these, BGP is guaranteed to converge. The export rule makes valid paths 'valley-free'.

Labovitz et al. (SIGCOMM 2000) injected faults at exchange points and found BGP took minutes to converge after failures, exploring many temporary paths; the delay comes from path exploration interacting with timers (MinRouteAdvertisementInterval, suggested 30 s for eBGP) and implementation choices.

Route redistribution copies routes between protocols (e.g., BGP or static into OSPF); metrics do not translate, and redistributing in both directions at two points can create routing loops unless tagged and filtered.

RFC 7908 defines a route leak as propagation of routing announcements beyond their intended scope, typically violating the customer/peer/provider export rules (e.g., a customer re-announcing one provider's routes to another).

June 24, 2019: DQE (AS33154) used a BGP optimizer that generated more-specific routes; its customer Allegheny Technologies (AS396531) leaked them to Verizon (AS701), which accepted and propagated them; Cloudflare reported roughly 15% of its global traffic lost at the worst point.

Feb 24, 2008: Pakistan Telecom (AS17557) originated 208.65.153.0/24, a more-specific of YouTube's 208.65.152.0/22; PCCW (AS3491) propagated it and longest-prefix match pulled YouTube traffic worldwide. YouTube countered with /25s; PCCW withdrew AS17557's routes at about 21:01 UTC, around two hours after the start.

RPKI origin validation (RFC 6811): Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) bind a prefix, a maximum length and an origin AS. A route is Valid if a ROA covers it with matching origin and length, Invalid if a ROA covers it but none matches, NotFound if no ROA covers it.

RFC 9319 (BCP 185) recommends avoiding maxLength in ROAs except in specific cases: a loose ROA authorizes unannounced sub-prefixes that a forged-origin attacker (who prepends the real origin AS) can use.
ROV checks only the origin AS; it does not stop a forged path ending in the right origin, or leaks of validly originated routes.
ROA coverage: about 56% of routed IPv4 and 59% of IPv6 address blocks were covered by ROAs as of August 2025.

RFC 9234 (2022) adds BGP Roles negotiated in OPEN (provider, customer, peer, route server, RS client) and the Only to Customer (OTC) attribute (type 35); a route marked OTC must not be sent to a provider or peer, and a marked route arriving from a customer is treated as a leak. BIRD 2.0.11, FRR 8.4 and OpenBGPD 7.5 support it.

ASPA (Autonomous System Provider Authorization) lets an AS sign the list of its providers in the RPKI so receivers can verify the AS_PATH is valley-free and detect leaks and some forged paths; as of late 2026 it is still an Internet-Draft awaiting write-up, not an RFC.

Oct 4, 2021: a maintenance command unintentionally disconnected Facebook's backbone; DNS servers that could no longer reach the data centers withdrew their BGP advertisements by design, making Facebook's names unresolvable for about six hours.
MPLS forwards on short labels pushed by the ingress router; with RSVP-TE, explicit-path tunnels (LSPs) are signaled hop by hop and every router on the path keeps state for every tunnel through it.

Segment Routing (RFC 8402): the ingress puts an ordered list of segments (instructions) in the packet; per-flow state is kept only at the ingress of the SR domain. Prefix segments mean 'go to this node by the IGP shortest path' (ECMP-aware); adjacency segments mean 'leave by this specific link'. SR-MPLS encodes segments as MPLS labels; SRv6 encodes them as IPv6 addresses.
The Internet is made of tens of thousands of autonomous systems (independently administered networks, each with one routing policy and an AS number).
OSPFv2 carries IPv4 only; IPv6 needed a new version, OSPFv3. IS-IS added IPv6, traffic-engineering and segment-routing data as new TLVs.

Mitigations for route reflectors hiding paths include BGP add-path (advertising more than one path) and placing reflectors with the topology in mind; hot-potato routing picks the exit with the lowest IGP cost.

Meta reported that an audit tool meant to block dangerous commands had a bug and did not stop the backbone-disconnecting command; recovery was slowed because internal tools depended on the same network.
Distance-vector computation is the distributed Bellman-Ford algorithm (Bellman 1958, Ford-Fulkerson).

Under RSVP-TE a full mesh of tunnels between n edge routers is n(n-1) unidirectional LSPs (50 edges → 2,450); SR-MPLS core state is roughly one node segment per router plus local adjacency segments, independent of the number of paths. SRv6 segments are 128-bit IPv6 addresses (16 bytes each).

With poisoned reverse: round 1 B16 C2 D3; round 2 C16; round 3 D16.

pitfalls: Assuming MED is compared across different neighbor ASes — by default it is not.
Treating ROV as BGP security in full: it validates the origin only, not the path.
Using loose maxLength in ROAs, which re-opens sub-prefix hijacks under forged origin.
Two-way redistribution at two points without tags creates loops.
Believing BGP convergence is like IGP convergence: BGP path exploration takes tens of seconds to minutes.
Route reflectors hide alternate paths; this can break MED, hot-potato choices, and fast failover unless add-path or diverse-path is used.

transport-beyond-tcp-basics.fetchNote: Facts gathered via web search snippets of the RFC/draft text and paper abstracts on 2026-11-14 (RFC sites were not fetched directly through the proxy); long-stable textbook facts cross-checked against implementations' comments.

claims.text: TCP's current specification is RFC 9293 (2022), which obsoletes RFC 793; its connection state machine has 11 states (CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT).
The side that closes first waits in TIME-WAIT for 2×MSL so stray old segments die and its final ACK can be resent; busy servers that actively close accumulate TIME-WAIT entries.
Classic loss detection: three duplicate ACKs trigger fast retransmit; otherwise the retransmission timeout (RTO) fires. Reordering by more than three packets is mistaken for loss.

RACK-TLP (RFC 8985) detects loss by time, not by counting duplicate ACKs: a packet is deemed lost if a packet sent sufficiently later has been delivered and a reordering window (a fraction of min RTT, about min_RTT/4, adapted upward when DSACKs show spurious retransmits) has passed. A Tail Loss Probe resends the last segment after ~2 SRTT to turn tail losses into fast recovery instead of an RTO.
Classical PMTUD (RFC 1191) sets Don't Fragment and relies on ICMP 'Packet Too Big' messages; when middleboxes filter ICMP, big packets vanish silently — a PMTU black hole.

Packetization-layer PMTUD (RFC 4821 for TCP, RFC 8899 for datagram transports such as QUIC) probes with larger packets and treats their loss as the signal, so it does not depend on ICMP; RFC 8899 updates RFC 4821.
Mathis et al. (1997): steady-state Reno throughput ≈ (MSS/RTT)·C/√p with C ≈ 1.22 (periodic loss, every packet ACKed); the authors later argued (2019) the model is outdated for modern stacks.

Congestion-control families: loss-based (Reno, CUBIC) reduce on packet loss; delay-based (Vegas, Swift) react to rising RTT; rate/model-based (BBR) estimate bottleneck bandwidth and min RTT and pace; learning-based (Remy offline-optimized rules, PCC Vivace online optimization) search for good actions against a utility function.

CUBIC (RFC 9438, 2023, obsoletes RFC 8312) grows the window as W(t)=C·(t−K)³+W_max with C=0.4 and multiplicative decrease β=0.7; K=∛(W_max(1−β)/C). Growth depends on time since the last loss, not on RTT; a Reno-friendly region keeps it at least as aggressive as Reno with α=3(1−β)/(1+β).
Loss-based control fills whatever buffer sits at the bottleneck before it sees a loss, so a deep buffer turns into standing queueing delay ('bufferbloat').

BBR models the path by two numbers — bottleneck bandwidth (max filter over delivery-rate samples) and round-trip propagation time (min filter over ~10 s) — and aims to keep inflight ≈ BDP. ProbeBW cycles pacing gain (1.25 probe, 0.75 drain, then 1.0 for six rounds in v1); ProbeRTT briefly drops inflight to 4 packets to re-measure min RTT; Startup uses a high gain (2/ln2 ≈ 2.89 in v1).
BBRv3 is specified in the IETF CCWG Internet-Draft draft-ietf-ccwg-bbr (Experimental), adopted as a WG item in 2024 and still a draft in 2026.
BBR (v1) vs CUBIC fairness depends on buffer depth: BBR takes more bandwidth when buffers are shallow despite high loss, CUBIC does better when buffers are deep.

DCTCP (RFC 8257): switches ECN-mark when the instantaneous queue exceeds a threshold K; the sender keeps α ← (1−g)α + g·F with F the fraction of marked bytes per window (g = 1/16 typical) and cuts cwnd ← cwnd·(1−α/2) at most once per window. The SIGCOMM paper suggests K > C·RTT/7 and used K ≈ 65 packets at 10 Gb/s.

RFC 8257 says DCTCP is for controlled environments such as data centers and must not be deployed over the public Internet without additional measures, because it reacts to ECN differently from standard TCP (RFC 3168).

Swift (Google, SIGCOMM 2020) is delay-based AIMD toward a target delay using NIC hardware timestamps, keeping separate fabric and endpoint windows and using the minimum; deployed in Google data centers for years.

Learning-based congestion control remains largely research: Remy computes rules offline for an assumed range of networks; PCC Vivace adjusts rate online by measuring a utility of throughput, latency and loss. Surveys call the field immature, and performance outside the trained conditions is a known risk.

QUIC (RFC 9000) runs over UDP, implements streams, flow control, loss recovery and congestion control in user space, and integrates TLS 1.3 (RFC 9001); almost all of its header beyond a few bits, the connection ID and the packet number field is encrypted, and the packet number itself is header-protected.
QUIC streams are independent: a lost packet only stalls the streams whose data it carried, removing TCP's cross-stream head-of-line blocking for multiplexed HTTP (HTTP/3).

RFC 9002: QUIC packet numbers increase monotonically and are never reused, so retransmitted data goes in a new packet and the 'which copy was ACKed?' ambiguity disappears; ACK frames carry the ACK delay; loss is declared after a packet threshold of 3 or a time threshold of 9/8 × max(smoothed RTT, latest RTT); the default congestion controller resembles NewReno, but implementations commonly use CUBIC or BBR.
QUIC's initial window per RFC 9002 is min(10·max_datagram_size, max(14720 bytes, 2·max_datagram_size)).

A fresh TCP+TLS 1.3 connection needs 2 RTTs before the first request is sent with data (1 for TCP, 1 for TLS); QUIC combines them into 1 RTT, and with a resumption ticket can send 0-RTT data in the first flight.

0-RTT data can be replayed by an attacker and has weaker forward secrecy; it must not carry non-idempotent requests. HTTP's RFC 8470 defines the Early-Data header and 425 (Too Early) status for servers to refuse risky early requests.

QUIC connections are identified by connection IDs, not the address 4-tuple, so a client can migrate (e.g. Wi-Fi to cellular); the peer must validate the new path with PATH_CHALLENGE/PATH_RESPONSE before sending much there, and endpoints switch to fresh connection IDs to resist linking across paths.

Langley et al. (2017) reported QUIC at ~7% of Internet traffic and over 30% of Google's egress at the time; it was built in user space partly so it could evolve faster than kernel TCP and avoid middlebox ossification.

MPTCP v1 (RFC 8684, 2020, obsoletes RFC 6824) spreads one connection over several TCP subflows; the first subflow negotiates with MP_CAPABLE (exchanging keys), later subflows join with MP_JOIN authenticated by those keys; a data-sequence mapping reassembles the byte stream across subflows.

Coupled congestion control (RFC 6356, LIA) links the subflows' window increases so a multipath flow takes no more than a single-path TCP would on the best path at a shared bottleneck, while moving traffic away from congested paths.
Apple's iOS 7 (2013) used MPTCP for Siri — the first large-scale commercial deployment — so a session survived moving from Wi-Fi to cellular.

Wireless links lose packets to fading and interference, not only to congestion; loss-based control misreads those losses, so Wi-Fi and cellular do link-layer retransmission, which in turn adds variable delay and large buffers (cellular bufferbloat).
TCP's window field is 16 bits (64 KB max); the window-scale option negotiated in the SYN multiplies it (up to ~1 GB), which long, fast paths need because throughput ≤ window / RTT.
VXLAN encapsulation adds 50 bytes over IPv4 (outer Ethernet 14 + IP 20 + UDP 8 + VXLAN 8), so a 1500-byte underlay cannot carry 1500-byte inner packets without fragmentation or a larger underlay MTU.

Encrypting transport headers removes signals operators used to measure RTT and loss passively; QUIC defines a single optional 'spin bit' that endpoints may flip once per round trip as a voluntary latency signal.
CUBIC is the default congestion controller in the Linux, Windows and Apple TCP stacks.
Later BBR versions (v2, v3) use loss and ECN as signals alongside the bandwidth/RTT model, addressing v1's disregard of loss.
Measurements found many Internet paths strip, rewrite or block unknown TCP options, which is why new transport features are hard to deploy in TCP.
Worked: at 10 Gb/s and 100 ms a 1460-byte-MSS Reno flow needs a window of ~86,000 segments; after one halving, +1 per RTT takes ~43,000 RTTs ≈ 70 min to recover.

pitfalls: Treating three duplicate ACKs as proof of loss — multipath fabrics and wireless links reorder; RACK's time window is the modern fix.
Blocking all ICMP 'breaks' nothing visible until big packets black-hole; PLPMTUD is the robust answer.
Assuming BBR is 'fair' because it is model-based — v1 could starve CUBIC in shallow buffers and lose to it in deep ones.
Turning on DCTCP on an Internet-facing path: it expects ECN marks to mean something different from RFC 3168.
Putting non-idempotent requests (payments, POSTs) in 0-RTT.
Expecting MPTCP to sum bandwidth at a shared bottleneck — coupled control deliberately prevents that.
Thinking QUIC removes head-of-line blocking entirely: within one stream, order still holds.
